name: Kangxi Emperor
info: The Kangxi Emperor, born Xuanye, was the third emperor of the Qing dynasty. He reigned in China from 1661 to 1722, put down the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, brought Taiwan, Mongolia and Tibet under Qing rule and sponsored great works of scholarship.

facts.born: 4 May 1654 in Jingren Palace, the Forbidden City, Beijing, as Xuanye; third son of the Shunzhi Emperor and Empress Xiaokangzhang
facts.died: 20 December 1722; buried at the Eastern Tombs in Zunhua, Hebei
facts.role: Third emperor of the Qing dynasty, enthroned 7 February 1661 at the age of seven; under regents until he took personal control in 1669; reigned 61 years, until 1722
facts.known: the longest reign of any Chinese emperor; the suppression of the Revolt of the Three Feudatories; the annexation of Taiwan in 1683; the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia; campaigns against the Dzungars; the Kangxi Dictionary and other great compilations; the Chinese Rites controversy; the succession dispute among his sons

t: Enthroned at seven and ruling through regents until 1669, the Kangxi Emperor reigned for 61 years, the longest reign of any Chinese emperor.

He put down the Revolt of the Three Feudatories in 1681, took Taiwan in 1683, agreed a border with Russia at Nerchinsk in 1689 and fought the Dzungars in Mongolia and Tibet, with severe measures against some of those who resisted.
His later years were marked by a succession dispute among his sons, and historians still debate whether the Yongzheng Emperor took the throne legitimately.
dyk: Thomas Pereira taught the Kangxi Emperor to play the harpsichord, and he was the first Chinese emperor to play a western musical instrument.
ev: Xuanye, the future Kangxi Emperor, is born in the Forbidden City in Beijing
He is enthroned at the age of seven, with four regents holding actual power
He has the regent Oboi arrested and begins to take personal control of the empire
Qing forces end the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, which had lasted eight years
The Qing admiral Shi Lang defeats the Kingdom of Tungning off Penghu, and Taiwan becomes part of the Qing Empire
The Treaty of Nerchinsk fixes a border between Russia and China
Pope Clement XI condemns the Chinese rites, and Kangxi forbids Christian missions in China
The Kangxi Emperor dies, and his fourth son Yinzhen succeeds as the Yongzheng Emperor

sections.early:
The Kangxi Emperor was born on 4 May 1654 in Jingren Palace in the Forbidden City, Beijing, the third son of the Shunzhi Emperor and Empress Xiaokangzhang, and was given the name Xuanye. Beijing had fallen to peasant rebels led by Li Zicheng and then to the Manchus in 1644, when the five-year-old Shunzhi Emperor was installed on the throne. By 1661, when Shunzhi died, the Qing conquest of China proper was almost complete. Xuanye was enthroned on 7 February 1661, at the age of seven (or eight by East Asian reckoning). His era name, Kangxi, began to be used on 18 February 1662, the first day of the following lunar year.

Actual power stayed for six more years with four regents, Sonin, Suksaha, Ebilun and Oboi, whom Grand Empress Dowager Zhaosheng had appointed in the name of the Shunzhi Emperor. Sonin died, leaving Suksaha at odds with Oboi, and in the struggle Oboi had Suksaha put to death and seized absolute power as sole regent. The young emperor and the court acquiesced. In the spring of 1662 the regents ordered a Great Clearance in southern China, which evacuated the entire population from the seacoast to counter a resistance movement of Ming loyalists led by the Taiwan-based general Zheng Chenggong, also titled Koxinga. The Grand Empress Dowager raised the boy. Herbert Giles, drawing on contemporary sources, described him as fairly tall and well proportioned, fond of manly exercises, and devoting three months a year to hunting.
sections.rise:
In 1669 the Kangxi Emperor had Oboi arrested, with the help of his grandmother, the Grand Empress Dowager Zhaosheng, and began to take personal control of the empire. He named three matters of concern: flood control of the Yellow River, repair of the Grand Canal and the Revolt of the Three Feudatories in south China. The Grand Empress Dowager continued to influence him greatly, and he cared for her himself in the months before her death in 1688.

After the Qing takeover of China in 1644, large parts of the south and west had been given as fiefs to three Ming generals who aided the Qing. In 1673 these were held by Wu Sangui, Geng Jingzhong and Shang Zhixin. Against the advice of most of his advisers, Kangxi tried to force the feudal princes to give up their lands and retire to Manchuria, and the attempt set off a rebellion that lasted eight years. Wu Sangui's forces overran most of southwest China. Kangxi employed generals including Zhou Peigong and Tuhai, relied mainly on Han Chinese soldiers of the Green Standard Army while the Manchu Banners took a back seat, and granted clemency to common people caught up in the war. He meant to lead the armies himself, but his subjects advised against it. The revolt ended in victory for the Qing in 1681. For years afterwards Kangxi reflected on his mistakes and blamed himself in part for the loss of life.
sections.deeds:
In 1683 the naval forces of the Ming loyalists on Taiwan, organised under the Zheng family as the Kingdom of Tungning, were defeated off Penghu by some 300 ships under the Qing admiral Shi Lang. Koxinga's grandson Zheng Keshuang surrendered a few days later and Taiwan became part of the Qing Empire. The end of the stronghold allowed Kangxi to relax the Sea Ban and permit resettlement of the Fujian and Guangdong coasts. On the northern frontier, after border conflicts with Russia along the Amur, Qing forces, including former followers of Zheng Chenggong, took part in the siege of Albazin in 1685, and negotiations led to the Treaty of Nerchinsk of 1689, which agreed a border between Russia and China.

Kangxi also dealt with the Mongols. The Dzungar chief Galdan attacked the Khalkha Mongols in 1688, and the Khalkha royal families sought help from the Qing in return for submission to Qing authority. The Qing emerged as victors at Ulan Butung in 1690. In 1696 and 1697 Kangxi personally led campaigns against the Dzungars, the one military campaign in which he actively took part, and the western section of his army defeated Galdan's forces at Jao Modo; Galdan died the following year. In Tibet, the Dzungars took Lhasa in 1717 with an army of 6,000 and killed Lhazang Khan, and defeated a Qing army at the Salween River in 1718. The Qing did not take control of Lhasa until 1720, when Kangxi sent a larger force.
sections.opponents:
Some of Kangxi's measures were harsh. When the Chahar Mongol leader Abunai and his brother Lubuzung revolted in 1675 with 3,000 followers, the revolt was put down within two months and Abunai and all his followers were killed. Their title was abolished, all Chahar Mongol royal males were executed, even those born to Manchu Qing princesses, and the royal females were sold into slavery, except the Manchu Qing princesses. The Manchu clan Hoifan, in 1697, and the Manchu tribe Ula, in 1703, were annihilated after they rebelled against the Qing, according to Liliya M. Gorelova. To win support against Galdan, Kangxi stirred anti-Muslim feeling among the Mongols of Qinghai, claiming, falsely, that Chinese Muslims were plotting with Galdan and that Galdan had converted to Islam.

The Chinese Rites controversy brought a different quarrel. Kangxi had issued an Edict of Toleration in 1692, at the request of the Jesuit Thomas Pereira. The Jesuits argued that Chinese Christians could take part in Confucian ceremonies and ancestor worship, while the Dominicans condemned them as idolatry. Pope Clement XI sided with the Dominicans and in 1705 sent Charles-Thomas Maillard de Tournon to communicate a ban on the rites and to insist on a papal representative in Beijing. Kangxi refused, wishing to keep missionary activity under his own oversight. After the papal bull Ex illa die of 19 March 1715 condemned the rites, he forbade Christian missions in China as "causing trouble".
sections.last:
The last decades were troubled by the succession. In 1674 Empress Xiaochengren died giving birth to Yinreng, who was named crown prince at the age of two. Kangxi oversaw his upbringing personally, but Yinreng was said to have beaten and killed his subordinates, and his supporters, led by Songgotu, formed a "Crown Prince Party". In 1707 Kangxi stripped him of his position, and the oldest surviving son, Yinzhi, who had been put in charge of the house arrest, recommended the eighth prince, Yinsi, and asked that Yinreng be executed. Kangxi was enraged and stripped Yinzhi of his titles. Suspecting that Yinreng had been framed, he restored him in 1709. In 1712 Yinreng was accused of trying to force his father to abdicate; Kangxi deposed him again and announced that he would appoint no crown prince for the rest of his reign.

The 13th prince, Yinxiang, was placed under house arrest for cooperating with Yinreng, and Yinsi lost his titles. According to official records, on the evening of 20 December 1722 Kangxi called seven of his sons to his bedside. After he died, Longkodo announced that he had chosen the fourth prince, Yinzhen, who took the throne as the Yongzheng Emperor. Kangxi was entombed at the Eastern Tombs in Zunhua, Hebei. It is debated whether he chose Yinti, the 14th prince, and Yinzhen forged the will in his own favour, or whether Yinzhen ascended legitimately.
sections.legacy:
Kangxi completed the conquest, suppressed all significant military threats and revived the central government system inherited from the Ming with important modifications. His reign began the period known as the High Qing era, or the "Prosperous Era of Kangxi and Qianlong". He devised the Palace Memorial System of secret messages between him and trusted officials, from which a Grand Council emerged, leaving the mandarin civil servants with routine administration. To win over Confucian scholars, many of them loyal to the Ming, he issued the Sacred Edict in 1670, held the civil service examinations every three years and sponsored the Ming Official History, the Kangxi Dictionary, the Complete Tang Poems and the Complete Classics Collection of Ancient China.

The national treasury held 14,930,000 taels in 1668 and about 50,000,000 between 1702 and 1709, then fell to 32,622,421 by 1721, a decline attributed to military expense and growing corruption. In 1712 he froze the land tax and corvée; the dynasty later suffered from this policy, since it preserved tax rates in perpetuity and hindered later attempts at reform. S. E. Finer wrote that Kangxi's own reflections show how "intimate and caring" his relations with the rank and file were.

summary: The Kangxi Emperor (1654-1722), enthroned at seven, reigned in China for 61 years, the longest reign of any Chinese emperor. He crushed the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, took Taiwan, fought the Dzungars and sponsored great compilations, while a succession dispute darkened his last years.
references: Robert B. Oxnam, Ruling from Horseback: Manchu Politics in the Oboi Regency, 1661–1669 (University of Chicago Press, 1975)
William T. Rowe, China's Last Empire: The Great Qing (Harvard University Press, 2009)
Jonathan D. Spence, Emperor of China: Self Portrait of K'ang Hsi (Vintage Books, 1975)
notes: Birth/accession: the article says enthroned 7 February 1661; era name used from 18 February 1662. Reign of 61 years is the lede's figure; not recomputed.

Yinreng is called both 'second surviving son' and, in the family list, 'seventh (second) son'; I say only 'Yinreng'. His age 'two' when named crown prince is as given. The article's accusations of incest and of buying children are left out (stated without attribution); only 'said to have beaten and killed subordinates' is kept.
Yinti is spelled 'Yinti (or Yinzheng)' in the dispute sentence, and the family list gives Yunti; 'Yinti' used. The family list also gives Yinzhi/Yunzhi forms; those in the body text used.
The Muslim passage: the article itself says Kangxi 'falsely' claimed; kept as 'claiming, falsely'.
Hoifan and Ula: only 'believed by Gorelova' to be linked to the Xibe relocation is hedged; the annihilation is stated flatly in the article, attributed here to Gorelova to be safe.
Tibet: the article says the lede 'incorporated Tibet'; the Lhazang Khan regent appointment (1705) and Sangye Gyatso concealing the Dalai Lama's death were left out for space.
'Considered one of China's greatest emperors' is the article's lede, kept as the article's own (unattributed) assessment.
The Eight Banners, Tong clan false claim, treasury figures for other years, Jesuit and scientific work, Matteo Ripa and porcelain left out for space.
The article has no place of death.
References left empty for the editor.
